subject: Architecture
title: The Lotus Temple: Architecture Without Borders
description: A short lesson to help you apply The Lotus Temple: Architecture Without Borders.

hook.text: The Lotus Temple in Delhi welcomes everyone — any faith, any nationality, no sermons allowed.

buildup.text: Twenty-seven marble 'petals' form a lotus flower shape that shelters 2,500 worshippers in silence.

discovery.text: Iranian architect Fariborz Sahba designed it for the Bahá'í faith, which teaches unity of all religions.

twist.text: It attracts more visitors than the Taj Mahal — over 10 million per year — despite no guided tours.

climax.text: The building has won numerous architectural awards and uses no straight lines anywhere.

punchline.text: No priests. No sermons. Just a flower made of stone and silence.

quiz.question: What religion does the Lotus Temple belong to?

details.summary: The Lotus Temple in New Delhi, designed by Fariborz Sahba and completed in 1986, uses 27 free-standing marble-clad petals to create a flower form. As a Bahá'í House of Worship, it welcomes all faiths — over 100 million visitors have entered since opening, more than the Taj Mahal in the same period.
details.whyItMatters: The Lotus Temple demonstrates that architecture can transcend religious boundaries. Its universal flower form avoids specific religious symbolism.
takeaways: 27 marble-clad petals create a lotus flower form
Over 100 million visitors since 1986 — more than the Taj Mahal
Welcomes all faiths as a Bahá'í House of Worship

faq.question: How were the lotus petals constructed?
faq.answer: Each petal is a thin reinforced concrete shell clad in Greek marble panels. The 27 petals are arranged in groups of three — nine outer petals, nine middle, and nine inner — creating three layers that open toward the central hall. Complex geometry required custom formwork for each shell.

faq.question: Can you explain: Why a lotus shape?
faq.answer: The lotus flower is sacred across multiple religions and cultures — in Hinduism, Buddhism, Islam, and others it symbolizes purity and divine beauty. Architect Sahba chose it to represent the Bahá'í principle of the oneness of religion through a universally recognized spiritual symbol.
